newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tough on NATO before Lisbon summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tough on NATO before Lisbon summit.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin took a tough line against NATO's plans to expand eastwards on Friday, three days before a European security summit.

"Russia's stance on NATO expansion remains unchanged, that is, negative," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky quoted Yeltsin as saying in a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
"Even if some want it or not, NATO expansion will lead to new divisions in Europe."

Yeltsin's remarks before Monday's start of the Lisbon summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) brought to a crescendo Russia's criticism this week of NATO plans to take in countries from eastern and central Europe.
Russia says NATO's expansion towards its borders would threaten its security. It wants the OSCE to play a wider security role in Europe and act as a counterbalance to NATO.
Chernomyrdin, who will head the Russian delegation to Lisbon, attacked NATO's plans during a visit to Paris this week.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said in a newspaper interview published on Thursday that one option for responding to NATO expansion would be to point Russia's missiles at eastern Europe.

"It could even come to us redirecting our missles at certain European countries entering NATO (all the more so if these countries agree to alliance nuclear weapons being positioned on their territory)," he told Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
Although Rodionov made clear that such an option was a radical one, it illustrated Moscow's deep concern over the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans.

It also signalled a switch back to tough rhetoric against the Western alliance. Although Moscow has constantly opposed NATO enlargement, it has wavered between outspoken criticism and much softer opposition in the last few months.
Russian officials have been working hard to ensure that none of the declarations agreed in Lisbon include statements that could be interpreted as support for NATO enlargement.

They have made clear that their opposition to NATO growth will become fiercer if Moscow is isolated at the OSCE summit. They have also said talks on limiting conventional arms will get tougher if there is no progress on that issue in Lisbon.

Moscow wants to create a pan-European security system which is free of blocs and divisions, guarantees equal security to all participants and controls arms levels on the continent. The OSCE would play a key role in this.

Yeltsin, meeting Cheneomyrdin and Primakov at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where he is recovering from heart surgery, said the Lisbon summit should help create the "new architecture of European security".
He praised the OSCE as a "universal and multifaceted organisation."
But most other countries have rejected Russia's plans, raising the prospect of confrontation at the two-day summit.
Yeltsin's opposition to NATO expansion plans helped wreck the last OSCE summit in Budapest in 1994.

The 65-year-old president will not be in Lisbon so soon after his operation on November 5. But Chernomyrdin and Primakov will have an influential nationalist lobby at home to consider when they are at the summit.
